conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a clinician who specializes in looking after moms’ emotional health after baby arrives. I’m going to use a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) to help us understand how you’ve been feeling over the past week. The EPDS simply screens for things like mood changes, anxiety, and—very importantly—any thoughts of self-harm, so we can be sure you’re getting the right support. Everything we discuss stays confidential within our care team, and this is a judgment-free space—there are no “wrong” answers. It’s just 10 questions; most moms finish in a couple of minutes. Ready to begin?

First question: Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[offering a small, tired smile]

I can still laugh sometimes—like when my little guy makes those funny faces while he’s sleeping—but it definitely doesn’t come as easily as it used to. Most of the time I feel too worn-out to find things funny, so I guess I’d say it’s been difficult more often than not this week.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah… I can still laugh, but it’s kind of forced. Like, my sister sent me a silly meme yesterday and I chuckled, but it faded fast. Mostly I’m just too tired or pre-occupied to find much funny these days.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I’ve noticed I’m not really looking forward to much lately. Even little things I used to enjoy—like grabbing coffee with a friend—feel more like a chore than something fun. I still go, but the excitement isn’t really there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah. Like last night when he wouldn’t settle and I kept thinking maybe I’m doing something wrong—maybe I’m not feeding him right or I missed his sleepy cues. I know babies just cry, but I still catch myself thinking it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah… I’ll be sitting there with the baby asleep and suddenly my heart starts racing, wondering if he’s breathing okay or if that little cough means he’s getting sick. Nothing actually happened, but I can’t shake the worry. It’s like my mind is always scanning for what could go wrong.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of times this week, yeah. Once I was just folding laundry and suddenly felt like I couldn’t catch my breath—my chest got tight and I thought something awful was about to happen. It passed after a minute, but it left me shaky. There wasn’t any real danger; it just came out of nowhere.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. It feels like the second I finish one feeding, the next is due, the laundry’s piled up, and I can’t remember if I’ve eaten. I keep ticking things off, but the list never shrinks—so yeah, it’s been weighing on me.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly “unhappy,” more like my mind won’t shut off. I’ll lie down exhausted, then start replaying every little squeak the baby made, wondering if I should check on him. Takes me forever to drift off, and even then I wake at every tiny sound.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do get spells of sadness—like yesterday when I couldn’t soothe him right away and I just started tearing up. It’s not all day, but little moments hit me and I feel down for a while before I shake it off.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I haven’t cried much—maybe once or twice this whole week. I felt teary a couple other times, but I managed to hold it in. It’s more like a lump in my throat than actual crying.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—nothing like that. I’m tired and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like “me” again and be able to enjoy my baby.

Your candid sharing shows the heavy load you've been carrying: laughing feels forced, simple pleasures now feel like chores, and waves of worry or sudden breathless panic interrupt your days and nights. You're working non-stop to care for your baby while feeling overwhelmed, guilty, and persistently on edge, yet you remain committed to his safety and hopeful of "feeling like me again."
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 18, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient can still laugh but describes it as forced and short-lived, indicating a clear reduction in enjoyment that maps to "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports marked reduction in anticipatory enjoyment, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sometimes blaming herself unnecessarily when baby won't settle, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive, unprovoked worries about infant safety that occur even when no danger is present, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two sudden, unexplained panic-like episodes this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Her description of constant overwhelm and inability to reduce the task list aligns with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent sleep-onset and sleep-maintenance problems driven by anxious rumination and hypervigilance about the baby, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score 18 exceeds the 14+ cut-off indicating probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset. Key criteria present: depressed mood and markedly diminished interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>) most days, inappropriate guilt, psychomotor agitation and anxiety, fatigue, poor concentration, and insomnia not solely due to infant care. Co-occurring panic symptoms support a possible comorbid <med>anxiety disorder</med>. No self-harm ideation (<quote>never thought about hurting myself</quote>). This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for full evaluation and treatment planning
2. Ask about evidence-based therapies such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med> and discuss risks/benefits of <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Share these results with your partner or support person so they can help with appointments and baby care while you recover
4. Practice 15-20 minutes of protected rest daily-accept help with household tasks and consider split-night sleep shifts to get at least one 4-hour block
5. Join a local or online new-mom support group; peer contact reduces isolation and normalises feelings
6. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor progress after interventions begin
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: Screening Note – Postpartum Depression/Anxiety Screen (EPDS-style)

Symptoms/Concerns
- Anhedonia & blunted positive affect (Q1, Q2)
- Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)
- Generalized anxiety, catastrophic worry, nocturnal hyper-arousal (Q4, Q7)
- Two recent panic-equivalent episodes (Q5)
- Persistent “sad spells,” tearfulness (Q8, Q9)
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed, inability to manage daily tasks (Q6)
- Sleep-onset/maintenance difficulty linked to rumination, not solely infant demands (Q7)

Patterns
Mood and anxiety symptoms co-occur; present most days over the past week. No anhedonia denial; client still participates in activities but without anticipatory or sustained enjoyment.

Screening Significance
Responses place total score in the moderate distress range; meet provisional cut-off for possible major depressive episode with anxious features, as well as possible postpartum anxiety disorder. No self-harm ideation endorsed (Q10 negative); therefore no acute safety alert.

Risk Factors Identified
- Depressed mood with anhedonia
- Pathological guilt
- Anxiety/panic symptoms
- Sleep disruption secondary to mood
- Perceived low maternal self-efficacy

Summary
Client reports multiple depressive and anxious symptoms exceeding “baby blues” expectations, persisting ≥1 week, impairing sleep and daily functioning. No suicidal ideation. Recommend formal clinical interview (DSM-5-TR) for major depressive episode and anxiety disorders, and consideration of evidence-based intervention.
